questions.question: Q1. What makes a bioink suitable for extrusion bioprinting?

answers.a: It must have the highest possible viscosity at all shear rates.
answers.b: It must be shear-thinning so it extrudes easily yet holds printed roads.
answers.c: It must be Newtonian (constant viscosity regardless of shear).
answers.d: It must be colored for visibility during printing.

explanations.a: Incorrect — High viscosity at high shear rate would clog the nozzle.
explanations.b: Correct — Shear-thinning inks flow under nozzle pressure but rebuild structure after deposition.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Newtonian inks lack the structural recovery needed to hold roads.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Color is not a functional requirement.

questions.question: Q2. What does the printability window (1–100 Pa·s) tell you?

answers.a: Inks outside this range either puddle or under-extrude and tear.
answers.b: The ink only exists in this viscosity range.
answers.c: It is the same for all nozzle sizes.
answers.d: It applies only to Newtonian fluids.

explanations.a: Correct — Below 1 Pa·s, inks spread; above 100 Pa·s, they fail to extrude cleanly.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Inks can exist at any viscosity; this range is for *printability*.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Different nozzle diameters shift the operating shear rate.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Power-law fluids are the rule in bioprinting.

questions.question: Q3. In the Avrami kinetics model, what does the gel point represent?

answers.a: The moment when all liquid has solidified.
answers.b: The end of the printing process.
answers.c: The conversion fraction α = 0.5, where the stored modulus G' reaches the gel threshold.
answers.d: The temperature at which the ink changes color.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Full solidification is α = 1, not the gel point.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Gel point is a time, not a process marker.
explanations.c: Correct — The gel point is defined at α = 1/2 for mechanical purposes.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Gelation is a chemical/physical event, not a color change.

questions.question: Q4. Why is cell survival lower with a finer (narrower) nozzle?

answers.a: The nozzle heats up and damages cells.
answers.b: A narrower nozzle forces higher wall shear stress, shearing and killing cells.
answers.c: Fine nozzles require higher extrusion speeds.
answers.d: The cells are too small to pass through fine tips.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Heating is not the primary mechanism in extrusion.
explanations.b: Correct — Wall shear stress τ_wall is inversely proportional to R³, so narrow tips generate steep stress gradients.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Living cells easily transit even 200 µm orifices if shear is low.

questions.question: Q5. Which threshold defines when a printed scaffold can no longer support tissue load?

answers.a: When the mass M drops to zero.
answers.b: When the temperature exceeds body temperature.
answers.d: When the modulus E falls below E_min, the load-bearing floor.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Mechanical failure occurs long before full mass loss.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Temperature does not degrade the scaffold in vivo.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Viscosity is not a scaffold property after printing.
explanations.d: Correct — The scaffold fails structurally when stiffness drops below the tissue's regeneration load.

questions.question: Q6. Why does PLGA scaffold fail weeks while PCL lasts years?

answers.a: PCL degrades much slower (k_deg = 0.0005/day vs. 0.02/day) due to its longer polymer backbone.

explanations.a: Correct — The degradation rate constant k_deg directly determines the timescale.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Density does not determine degradation rate.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Thickness affects load-bearing floor, not inherent degradation.
explanations.d: Incorrect — PLGA is FDA-approved and widely used in implants.

questions.question: Q7. For a tracheal stent, why is the printed curvature deliberately set to 1.2× the target airway curvature?

answers.a: To ensure the stent is stronger than needed.
answers.c: To overcompensate for elastic spring-back so the stent seats firmly when deployed.
answers.d: Because the formula requires it mathematically.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Strength is not the issue; seating is.
explanations.c: Correct — The 20% overshoot accommodates relaxation and ensures the stent stays in place.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The multiplier is a design choice to guarantee mechanical fit.

questions.question: Q8. What is the critical role of shape fixity R_f > 95% in the deployment gate?

answers.a: It ensures the stent survives sterilization.
answers.c: It measures how fast the stent recovers its permanent shape.
answers.d: It guarantees the temporary (flat-printed) shape holds without external constraint until deployment.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Sterilization is not addressed by shape fixity.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Fixity is a material property, not a process parameter.
explanations.c: Incorrect — That is the role of shape recovery R_r.
explanations.d: Correct — High R_f means the stent stays flat during storage and transport, not deploying prematurely.

questions.question: Q9. Why is a glass transition T_g of 45–50°C dangerous for a bioprinted stent used in the airway?

answers.a: It is above body temperature, so the stent can never deploy.
answers.b: It is too close to body temperature (37°C), risking premature unwanted deployment during room-temperature storage.

explanations.a: Incorrect — 45–50°C is above 37°C, so deployment will occur.
explanations.b: Correct — A stent with T_g = 35°C (PCL-based) is only 2°C below body temp, risking activation during handling.
explanations.c: Incorrect — T_g is not melting; it is the glassy-to-rubbery transition.
explanations.d: Incorrect — T_g is set during synthesis, not printing.

questions.question: Q10. Which SMP material clears all three deployment safety gates for the tracheal stent?

answers.a: PLA-SMP with T_g = 58°C, R_f = 97%, and R_r = 92%.
answers.d: Any shape memory polymer with T_g > 37°C.

explanations.a: Correct — PLA-SMP meets all gates: T_g = 58°C (safe margin from 37°C), R_f = 97% > 95%, R_r = 92% > 90%.
explanations.b: Incorrect — PCL-SMP T_g = 35°C is too close to body temperature; fixity is also below threshold.
explanations.c: Incorrect — R_r = 88% falls below the 90% requirement.
explanations.d: Incorrect — T_g > 37°C is necessary but not sufficient; fixity and recovery must also be high.
